newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Mkt attention on FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Mkt attention on FOMC meeting.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's policy-making arm will decide whether it believes the U.S. economy continued to grow at an unsustainable pace when it meets on Tuesday.

The Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday and economists were divided as to whether it would vote to raise short-term interest rates by another 25 basis points or hold off until it sees further evidence of strong consumer spending. The Fed hiked rates at its last meeting but some softening has been seen in recent statistics.

Following the last FOMC meeting, the Fed issued a statement indicating it would move to tighten monetary policy even if no blatant inflationary signs were seen if consumer spending continued at a rapid pace. Retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April, giving the Fed some leeway to pause, economists said.

On Friday the market was pressured by a weakening dollar versus the yen. Gary Ciminero, economist at Independent Economic Advisors, said the dollar's fall was inflationary and could lead to further tightening. He expected to see the Fed tighten again on Tuesday.

Long-term prospects were for increasing capacity utilization and a further tightening of the labor market, even though capacity utilization fell slightly in April and industrial production was unchanged, Ciminero said.

"There's not a lot of data beyond the decision by the Fed next week. Our estimation is it's a close call, but the Fed remains on hold," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.
Kretzmer said some recent signs of slowing demand and a continued good inflationary scenario were putting no pressure on the Fed to rush into another tightening.
"The market has priced the Fed in about right at this point. We could see a bit of a bounce based on (Friday's) losses, but most of the week should be a technical trade," Kretzmer said.

He said it was unlikely bond prices would move out of current ranges near-term as it was questionable whether recent slowdowns in consumer demand were temporary or an aberration of the high levels seen in recent quarters.
"Is the slowdown long-lasting or likely to be reversed? The Fed could be back in the (tightening) saddle by July," Kretzmer said.
Ward McCarthy, managing director at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc, and formerly an economist at the Richmond Fed, saw the Fed refraining from tightening.

"I don't think the market will respond in any significant fashion at all. The (current) risk/reward scenario puts the market at some peril if the Fed does decide to move," McCarthy said. He added the federal funds futures contract was one indication that the market had dismissed a further tightening.
The only major market concern other than the Fed would be supply, with Treasury announcing the size of its next two- and five-year sales on Wednesday.
In late trading Friday, the 30-year bond was down 16/32 at 96-14/32 to yield 6.91 percent.
At the short end the three-month bill was up seven basis points at 5.05 percent. The six-month was up seven basis points at 5.35 percent and the year bill was up three basis point at 5.53 percent.
Ten-year notes were down 9/32 at 99-15/32 to yield 6.70 percent. Five-year issues were down 5/32 at 100-10/32 to yield 6.55 percent and two-years were off 2/32 at 100-07/32 to yield 6.25 percent.
